_comment: Feature 006 — the committed source of the in-app client changelog. Ingested at agent boot and via POST /admin/content/reingest. Each entry upserts by `slug` (idempotent). Client-facing register: keep it tester-friendly, no dev detail. A live Admin -> Updates edit of the same slug wins over this file.

entries.title: Beta polish — Robinhood Chain throughout, clearer states, smoother loading
entries.body:
A round of production polish for the Robinhood Chain beta.

The app now consistently says "Robinhood Chain" (with its logo) rather than any leftover test-network wording, and swaps route through Uniswap. Features that aren't live yet — the yield vault, the utility token, the Sparky Broker — now show a clean "not available yet" note instead of test data. The sign-in screen no longer flickers while it checks your access, the swap lets you add any token by pasting its address, and Sparky now describes exactly what's available on this network.

We also restored the assistant's knowledge search, which had quietly gone offline.

entries.title: The beta now runs on Robinhood Chain — sign in, chat, portfolio and swaps are live
entries.body:
beta.sparkpoint.io now runs on Robinhood Chain mainnet — and only Robinhood Chain. Connect a wallet on Robinhood Chain, sign in, chat with Sparky, see your live portfolio, and swap between ETH and USDG through the network's own on-chain Uniswap V3. During the beta the swap takes no fee.

A few things are intentionally switched off for now and shown as "coming soon": the utility token, the Sparky Broker, and the yield vault. They arrive in a later step, once their contracts are deployed. Everything you can use today runs against the real network with your own wallet — you are always the only one who can move your funds.

entries.title: The assistant now recovers on its own after a database restart
entries.body:
If the database behind the assistant was restarted — during maintenance, or after a server reboot — the assistant used to get stuck: it couldn't reconnect on its own, so chat history, tips and other saved data kept failing until someone manually restarted it.

Now it heals itself. The moment the database is back, the next request quietly re-establishes the connection, and while the database is briefly unavailable the health check reports that honestly instead of pretending everything is fine.

Nothing changes day to day — this just removes a way the assistant could go quietly dark after routine infrastructure restarts.

entries.title: Groundwork for Robinhood mainnet is now wired in
entries.body:
Following on from getting the app ready for Robinhood mainnet, we've now wired the network into the core plumbing — the address book, the safety/policy layer, and the assistant's chain settings all recognise Robinhood Chain now, entirely fail-closed.

That means nothing is switched on for it yet (no token, no vault, no trading on that network) and nothing changes for you today. It's the quiet groundwork so that when the mainnet beta's contracts go live, turning it on is a configuration change rather than new code.

entries.title: Getting the app ready to run on Robinhood mainnet
entries.body:
Until now, parts of the app quietly assumed the test network everywhere — which network to show when your wallet wasn't connected, which explorer the "view transaction" links pointed at, and which network the admin tools talked to were all fixed to Base Sepolia.

That's fine while there's only a test environment, but the beta is going live on Robinhood Chain, and the same code runs in both places. So every screen now follows whichever network the build is pointed at, in one place, instead of each screen deciding on its own.

Nothing changes for you on the test network — it behaves exactly as before. On the mainnet beta, links and network labels will correctly point at Robinhood Chain rather than the test network. No action needed.

entries.title: The testnet bots ran on time for ten hours and did nothing
entries.body:
The scheduled job that drives testnet activity fired punctually every hour overnight and accomplished nothing at all.

Scheduled jobs run with a much smaller set of system paths than a normal login session, and the program that runs the bots was not on it. Each cycle failed on its first step, wrote two tidy lines saying it had degraded, and exited reporting success. From the outside it looked like a healthy schedule.

What caught it was the operator panel added the day before. Because no cycle ever completed, no run was ever filed, and the panel showed both jobs as overdue by nearly ten hours — which is exactly the state it was built to make visible. Nothing was lost; the bots simply had not run.

The runner now locates the program properly, and refuses to start at all if it cannot — loudly, rather than pretending a cycle happened.

entries.title: The bot panel showed a permanent warning for a job that was never scheduled
entries.body:
Admin → System → Activity bots listed three jobs and showed one of them — the vault deposit job on Base Sepolia — as "never run", permanently.

Nothing was broken. That job simply is not part of the hourly schedule: it is a one-off setup step used to put funds into the vault, and the bot wallets are already at their per-wallet deposit limit, so it could not have done anything even if it had run.

The panel was listing it as though it were expected to run, which made a completed setup step look like a stalled job. A warning that can never clear is one people learn to scroll past, and then they scroll past a real one — so this was worse than showing nothing.

The list now reflects what is actually scheduled, and a check keeps the two from drifting apart again. If the vault job is ever run, it still appears.

entries.title: The vault fee reader was crashing on startup, invisibly
entries.body:
Yesterday's note said the piece that records the vault's performance fee had been switched on. It had — and then it crashed the instant it started, every single time, without leaving a trace.

One small library was missing from the server image: the component that computes the cryptographic fingerprints used to recognise events on the blockchain. The reader needs it the moment it loads, so it failed immediately. Because of how background jobs report problems, that failure was thrown away silently — no error, no warning, nothing in the logs.

From the outside it looked exactly like a vault that had earned nothing, which is the most misleading way a system can fail.

The missing library is now installed, a check refuses any future build that drops it, and background jobs now report their own death instead of disappearing quietly. That last part is what found this one.

entries.title: The bot monitor could not receive the reports it was built to show
entries.body:
The panel that shows whether the testnet bots are running went live yesterday and immediately could not be told anything: every report the runner sent came back rejected.

The cause was one wrong line. The endpoint asked to be authenticated using a helper that was never meant to be wired up that way, and the web framework quietly reinterpreted it as asking for a value in the web address rather than in the request's credentials. Every report failed with a complaint about a missing field that the runner had no way to supply.

Nothing was lost — a report that cannot be filed is only telemetry, and the bots themselves kept working throughout. But the panel showed "never run" for a fleet that was running, which is exactly the wrong answer for a screen whose whole job is telling those two apart.

The route is now tested through a real request rather than only in pieces, because that is the only kind of test that would have caught it.

entries.title: The operator panel can now see whether the testnet bots are running
entries.body:
SparkPoint runs a small fleet of bots on the test networks so the revenue and portfolio screens have real activity to show before the first testers arrive.

Those bots deliberately run outside the app. SparkPoint's backend holds no keys and signs nothing — that is a promise the whole non-custody design rests on — so anything that signs transactions has to live somewhere else. The side effect was that nobody could tell, from inside the app, whether the fleet was working.

There is now a read-only view under System that answers it. It separates three things that otherwise look identical from the outside: never started, stopped, and running-but-achieving-nothing. The last one is the dangerous one — a fleet can report in perfectly on time while every action it attempts is being refused.

It is a mirror, not a remote control. There is no start or stop button, because adding one would mean the app could make something sign a transaction. The schedule stays where the keys are.

entries.title: The vault's performance fee was earning but never being recorded
entries.body:
SparkPoint's vault charges 10% of the yield it makes above its previous high-water mark. That part has always worked on chain.

What did not work was the recording. The piece that reads those fee events off the blockchain and files them was built, tested and then never switched on — so the revenue page had no way to show a performance fee even after one had been charged. Its position marker had sat at block zero since the day it was created, which is the giveaway: it had never read anything at all.

It now runs alongside the other two readers, checking every few minutes. Nothing about the fee itself changed — not the rate, not who receives it, not when it applies. Only whether anyone was writing it down.

Worth being plain about the size of it: the vault holds test funds and the amounts involved are fractions of a test dollar. This is about the plumbing being honest, not about the number.

entries.title: Applying for access is a calmer journey now
entries.body:
Three things about the new application form were more awkward than they needed to be.

Pressing “Apply for alpha access” on the front page used to fling the page down to the very bottom at high speed, racing the whole animation past on the way. It now simply opens the application page, the way a link should.

The form itself has moved off the bottom of the front page and onto that page. Ending “We can't touch your money — here's the proof” with four boxes to fill in made the closing point feel like paperwork. The front page now offers the two doors side by side — connect your wallet if you already have access, or apply if you do not — and the form has its own address you can bookmark or share.

On shorter screens the top of the form was tucked underneath the menu bar and could not be scrolled back into view, so the heading was simply unreachable. It now always sits clear of it.

And the “What's new” pop-up no longer appears over the application page. If you are there, you are trying to ask for access, not read our release notes.

entries.title: Applying no longer loses your answers if you are quick
entries.body:
If you filled in the new application form and pressed Apply before the page had completely finished loading, the page reloaded itself and everything you had typed disappeared — no message, no explanation, just an empty form again. Most people would have assumed the form was broken, and some would not have tried a second time.

This was most likely to happen on the front page, which loads an animation and therefore takes the longest to become ready.

The Apply button now stays switched off for the moment before the page is ready, and switches on by itself. Being unable to press it for an instant is a great deal better than losing four fields of typing. Once the page is ready, both clicking and pressing Enter work exactly as you would expect.

We found this by using the form ourselves on the live site rather than only testing the pieces underneath it.

entries.title: Tightened the anti-spam safeguard on the new application form
entries.body:
The application form we shipped today limits how many requests can come from one connection in an hour, so nobody can flood the review queue and bury real applications.

After it went live we tested that limit against the real site rather than trusting it, and found the check could be sidestepped: it was reading a piece of information the visitor's own browser could set freely, so anyone could simply present a different value each time and skip the limit entirely. It now only trusts that information where it comes from a source that cannot be faked.

The same test confirmed the good news, which is why it was worth running: the limit correctly tells different visitors apart. A rush of genuine applicants will not be mistaken for one person, and nobody will be turned away because somebody else applied first.

Nothing about applying changed, and no application was affected.

entries.title: You can now ask for alpha access without connecting a wallet
entries.body:
Until today, the only way to request access was to connect a wallet, sign a message, and be told your wallet is not in the alpha yet — and only then were you offered a form. That is backwards. Somebody who has just heard about Sparky has no reason to connect a wallet to a product they cannot use, so the form existed for people who could not reach it.

There is now an application form on the front page itself, and on its own address at /apply so it can be shared directly. You type the wallet address you would like whitelisted, tell us how to reach you and why, and that is it. Nothing to install, nothing to sign, no wallet involved.

One thing we want to be plain about, because it is the honest limitation of asking rather than proving: since nobody signs anything, an address typed into this form is a claim. So each application tells the reviewer which kind it is — signed-in, or typed in — and an approval is still a person reading it and deciding. Submitting grants nothing on its own, moves no funds, and cannot change or overwrite an application somebody else already sent for the same address.

We will reply on whichever contact you give us.

entries.title: Revenue share is now in the menu
entries.body:
The revenue share page existed and worked, but nothing in the app linked to it — you could only get there by typing the address. That is fixed: it is now under Information, directly below Sparky Broker, and the ⌘K search finds it if you type “revenue”, “claim” or “payout”.

Our automated check missed this because it opens each page by its address, so the page looked perfectly healthy while being effectively invisible. The check now clicks through the menu instead, so a page that nothing links to will fail rather than pass.

entries.title: Revenue share ran end to end on the testnet
entries.body:
We funded a real pot on the test network and ran the whole thing: the money went in, the split was calculated from who actually holds an activated broker, and holders claimed their shares on-chain.

Two things we specifically wanted to prove, and did. A second attempt to claim the same period fails — nobody can take their share twice. And a holder who did not claim straight away could still claim in full after the next period had already opened: your share is set aside for you and does not expire.

A note on older brokers: a couple were activated before the tier system existed, so they have no tier recorded. Rather than charge those holders again or leave them out, they count at 1.0×. Where that applies, the claim page says so on screen, and the published breakdown marks exactly which brokers it applied to.

Every period’s full breakdown is published so anyone can check the maths themselves against the blockchain — no login needed to read it. Claiming remains switched off for live revenue; there is still nothing real to distribute.

entries.title: Two activated brokers were invisible to the revenue split
entries.body:
While testing the revenue-share plumbing against the real blockchain, we found that two brokers which are genuinely activated were not showing up in the calculation at all — not as included, and not as excluded. They were simply invisible.

The cause: they were activated using an older version of our activation contract, which announces activations in a slightly different format than the current one. Our code was only listening for the new format.

We now build the list from the collection’s full ownership history instead, so a broker cannot be missed regardless of which version activated it.

We also found that those two brokers have no tier weight recorded anywhere, because the older contract predates tiers entirely. Rather than quietly leaving them out of any future split, the system now refuses to calculate one at all until a person decides how they should be treated. Nothing has been distributed and nothing is owed today, but a published split cannot be undone, so we would rather stop than guess.

entries.title: We now catch out-of-date wording before it reaches you
entries.body:
Twice recently the app showed wording that was no longer true — the Premium card still said “10,000 SRK /mo” after that pricing was retired, and the SRK page said the faucet lived on the Premium page after it had moved.

Both slipped through because our automated search looked at the code, and in the code those sentences are broken into pieces. The page reads “10,000 SRK /mo”; the code has the price and the “/mo” in two separate places, so searching for the sentence found nothing.

There is now a check that reassembles the text the way you would actually read it, and it runs on every change before it can be merged. A second check loads the real site each week and reads the pages the same way, which catches wording that comes from our servers rather than the code.

Both are built so they cannot quietly pass: if a page fails to load, that is reported as a broken check rather than a clean one.

entries.title: Your brokers list loads without scanning the whole collection
entries.body:
The Brokers page used to find your brokers by checking every token in the collection one by one. That works when there are a handful of them and would not have worked at ten thousand.

It now asks an index built from the blockchain’s own transfer history instead, so the page stays fast no matter how large the collection gets.

The old method is still there as a backup. If the index cannot be reached, the page falls back to reading the chain directly from your browser rather than showing you an empty list — we would rather it be slow than have it tell you that you own nothing when you do.

entries.title: There is now a page for revenue share
entries.body:
You can find it at Brokers → Revenue share. Right now it will tell you that nothing has been distributed, because nothing has.

We built the page in that state on purpose. It reads the contract directly and reports what is actually there, so when a period is eventually funded and published you will see the real amount rather than a promise. It shows no estimates, no monthly figures and no projected returns — the only number it will ever display is what the contract says you can claim at that moment.

If nothing is claimable it also tells you which reason applies: no period has been opened, a period exists but has not been published yet, this wallet was allocated nothing, or you have already claimed. Those are different situations and we would rather be specific than leave you guessing.

entries.title: The brokers list works — and loads about twice as fast
entries.body:
The new way of loading your brokers did not work the first time it ran on the live site, even though every test passed. Our blockchain connection limits how much history it will return in one request, and the limit is much lower than the one the blockchain itself allows — so the page kept asking for more than it was allowed and gave up.

It now works out the allowed size for itself and remembers it, and fetches the pieces at the same time rather than one after another. Loading a wallet’s brokers went from about eight seconds to about three.

Worth noting: while it was failing, the page did not tell you that you owned nothing. It said it could not read the chain and fell back to the older method. That was deliberate, and it is why nobody saw an empty collection.

entries.title: The revenue-share contract is deployed — and switched off
entries.body:
Activating a Sparky Broker records a payout weight. Until now there was nothing on the other end of that weight. There is now a contract deployed on Robinhood testnet that can hold a pot and pay it out to broker holders in proportion to their weight.

We want to be exact about what that does and does not mean, because this is the part people misread.

Nothing is claimable. No money has been put in, no allocation has been published, and claiming stays impossible until someone publishes one. We did not add an on/off switch for this — the contract simply cannot pay out until a period is published, which is a stronger guarantee than a setting we promise not to flip.

There is no way for us to take the pot. The contract has no withdraw, no sweep and no rescue function — not for an admin, not for anyone. The only way value ever leaves it is a holder claiming their own share. Anything funded and not claimed stays put and rolls into the next period; it cannot be moved to a SparkPoint address, because no such path exists.

We are building the plumbing before there is anything to send through it, so that it is finished and checked when that changes. We are not promising income, a rate or a date.

entries.title: Activating a broker now has three tiers
entries.body:
When you activate a Sparky Broker you now choose a tier: Analyst (250,000 SRK), Associate (500,000) or Partner (1,000,000). The flat price is gone.

Read this part before you choose. All three tiers unlock exactly the same Premium — every feature, identical. The only difference is a larger payout weight recorded against your broker on the blockchain.

And we want to be blunt about what that weight does today: nothing. Revenue sharing is not built. There is no payout, no pot and no way to claim anything, so paying for Partner instead of Analyst costs you 750,000 more SRK and gets you nothing you can use right now. The only reason to choose a higher tier is if you specifically want the larger weight recorded for later, accepting that later may never come.

We would rather say that plainly than let the word \u201cweight\u201d do the implying.

entries.title: Premium is a broker you own, not a monthly bill
entries.body:
We have gone through the whole app and rewritten everywhere that still described Premium as a monthly SRK subscription. It is not one any more.

Premium now comes from a Sparky Broker you activate once. Nothing renews, nothing expires, and there is no date to remember — it stays on for as long as you hold the broker, and it ends if you sell it.

A few practical changes while we were in there. The SRK faucet has moved from the Premium page to the SRK page, under Information — SRK's job now is activating a broker, so it sits with the token rather than next to a price. Sparky Broker has its own entry in the sidebar under Information. And your Settings page now shows Sparky Brokers, telling you which broker is carrying your Premium.

One correction worth being straight about: some earlier copy suggested that activating a broker earns you a share of platform revenue. That is not something we have built, so we have removed the claim. If it ever ships, we will say so plainly rather than leave it implied.

entries.title: Premium now comes from a Sparky Broker
entries.body:
There is a new way to get Premium, and it is better than the one it replaces.

A Sparky Broker is one of 10,000 collectible desks on the SparkPoint floor. Minting one is free. Activating it retires 10,000 SRK — the same amount that used to buy a single month — and Premium then stays on for as long as you hold that broker. Nothing renews, nothing expires, and there is no date to remember.

The part worth understanding: the entitlement lives in the broker, not in your account. If you sell or transfer it, the activation clears and your Premium ends — and whoever receives it activates it themselves. That is deliberate. It is what makes a broker worth something to sell, and it is why we check the blockchain every time rather than writing your plan down somewhere.

An activated broker wears a gold frame. The picture and the entitlement are the same fact.

The old monthly SRK subscription is being retired in favour of this. Your Premium page now tells you which of the two is currently paying for your access, and what would end it.

entries.title: The SRK faucet now works on Robinhood Testnet too
entries.body:
The Get SRK faucet on the Premium page used to serve Base Sepolia only. It now serves Robinhood Testnet as well, from the same card — it follows whichever network your wallet is on, and you can look at the other one without switching first.

Why we did this: the Sparky Broker collection lives on Robinhood Chain, and activating a broker retires SRK. A blockchain transaction can only touch one network at a time, so for activation to happen in a single step — with no waiting and nothing for us to do on your behalf — the SRK has to live on the same network as the broker. This is that groundwork.

One thing worth knowing: each network has its own separate SRK. Balances do not carry across, and buying Premium still happens on Base Sepolia. If you are connected to Robinhood Testnet the Premium purchase page now says so plainly rather than offering you a payment that could not be completed.

entries.title: “Try again” now appears when an answer fails
entries.body:
When Sparky can't complete an answer you get a card saying something went wrong and that nothing was signed or changed. That part was right — but on the most common kind of failure the card asked you to try again without giving you a button to do it.

There are two ways a message can fail. If the request never reaches us, you had a Try again button. If it reaches us and the model doesn't answer — which is what usually happens, and is a fault at the model provider rather than in your wallet or your funds — the button was missing.

It's there now, in both cases, and it resends exactly what you typed. Nothing about your funds is ever involved in a failed answer.

entries.title: Chain reads are now resilient to provider outages
entries.body:
Everything SparkPoint reads from the blockchain — your portfolio, vault quotes, swap prices — now travels through a proxy we operate. If our data provider slows down or fails, requests retry against a backup automatically, so a provider having a bad day no longer shows up as errors on your screen.

Two more things changed under the hood. Data that can never change (confirmed history) is now answered from a cache instead of being fetched again and again. And the access key for our data provider no longer ships inside the app your browser downloads — it stays on our servers, where a key belongs.

One thing deliberately did NOT change: the Exit page still talks to the public network directly, never through anything we run. Your withdrawal path depends on no SparkPoint server — including the new one.

Our admin console also watches this proxy live — and when it can't reach it, it now says why, not just that it can't.

entries.title: Your messages now send one at a time
entries.body:
If you sent a second message while Sparky was still answering the first, both were being handled at once. That caused two problems.

In a brand-new chat, each of those messages started its own separate conversation. You'd see one thread on screen and find three in your sidebar afterwards, each named after a different message. In an existing chat, the replies could come back attached to the wrong questions, because neither message could see the other.

Now a message you send while Sparky is working waits its turn. You'll see it sitting there, dimmed, with a note saying how many are waiting, and it goes out as soon as the current answer finishes — in the order you typed.

The suggestion buttons also step out of the way while an answer is on its way. They're for suggesting what to ask next, and until the answer arrives there isn't a next yet.

If something goes wrong mid-way, anything still waiting is kept rather than sent into the same problem — it stays on screen with a button to send it when you're ready.

entries.title: Your chats are now grouped by when — and searchable
entries.body:
The conversation list in the sidebar is no longer one long column. It's grouped under Today, Yesterday, Previous 7 days, Previous 30 days, and then by month and year, with a count beside each heading and the time of each conversation on its row.

That last part matters more than it sounds: if you asked the same question five times, the five threads all had the same name and no way to tell them apart. We didn't rename them — you did ask the same thing — we just showed you when each one was.

There's also a search box, and it searches all of your chats rather than only the ones currently on screen.

And one honest correction: the list only ever showed your 50 most recent conversations, and nothing said so — it simply stopped. If you have more, you'll now see exactly how many and can load them.

entries.title: Reopened chats remember where they got to
entries.body:
The suggestion buttons under the message box now stay relevant when you come back to an older conversation.

Until now they only knew about a conversation while you were typing in it. Open one from the sidebar, or come back after a refresh, and they reset to the same generic starters — so a thread that had spent ten messages on fees would greet you with "What's in my wallet?", as though none of it had happened.

They now pick up from the last thing that was actually discussed. A genuinely empty conversation still gets the starters, because that one really is new.

entries.title: Sources now fold away, so the answer leads
entries.body:
Sparky still cites everything it uses — but the Sources card no longer takes up more room than the answer itself. It now appears folded, showing how many sources an answer rests on, and opens with one tap.

We didn't remove the citations, and we won't. Being able to check where an answer came from is the difference between an answer and a guess. What changed is only which of the two you see first.

If you'd rather always see them in full, there's a switch in Settings → Appearance: "Sources under answers". It's per device, so your phone and your laptop can differ.

entries.title: Sparky now suggests what to ask next
entries.body:
The suggestion buttons under the message box used to stay the same all conversation. Now they change based on what you were just talking about.

Ask about the performance fee and you'll be offered "When would I pay nothing?" and "What's the high-water mark?". Look at your portfolio and you'll be offered "Where's my risk concentrated?". You won't be offered the question you just asked — which is what used to happen, and it made Sparky look like it hadn't been listening.

The way out is always one of the options, sitting quietly at the end. You should never have to hunt for how to withdraw.

entries.title: Sparky now shows you what it's doing while it thinks
entries.body:
While Sparky works on an answer you'll now see the step it's actually on — reading your portfolio, checking its knowledge base, and so on — with a timer, instead of the word "Working…" and nothing else.

There's a bigger fix underneath it. Sparky's replies were supposed to arrive piece by piece, but something between the assistant and your browser was holding the whole reply back and delivering it in one go at the end. So a twenty-second answer looked like twenty seconds of nothing. That's fixed: the steps now appear as they happen.

We only found it because the old waiting message looked exactly the same whether anything was arriving or not. A placeholder that can't be wrong hides whether the thing behind it works.

entries.title: The system page was reporting an outage that wasn't happening
entries.body:
The admin System page had been showing "Base RPC — Down" since the end of July. The connection was fine the whole time.

A while back we renamed one of the health checks so it describes the network a deployment is actually on. The page kept asking for the old name, got nothing back, and displayed nothing as a failure. No error, no log — just a red light next to something that was working.

Beyond fixing the name, the page now tells the difference between "this is broken" and "we didn't get an answer about this". They look the same on a status board and they are not the same thing, and a page that raises false alarms is a page people stop reading — which is exactly when a real problem gets missed.

It also now shows whether the connected network is the one we expect. That check existed but was never displayed, and it's the one that matters most: a connection can answer perfectly while being pointed at the wrong network.

entries.title: A shorter admin menu
entries.body:
The admin panel's side menu is down from nineteen entries to nine. Screens you look at together are now tabs on one page rather than separate destinations.

Users & access holds user analytics, AI usage, the allowlist and tiers. Vault holds the live figures and the configuration. System holds status, uptime, diagnostics, the kill-switch and the audit log. Knowledge already worked this way.

The old grouping asked you to remember things: that the kill-switch wasn't under System, that a user's tier wasn't under Users. During an incident is a bad time to be remembering where something lives.

Nothing has been taken away, and every link you had still works — the old addresses now take you straight to the right tab.

entries.title: Sparky's research no longer competes with your chat
entries.body:
The daily research Sparky writes for itself now runs on its own model, separate from the one that answers you.

Before this they shared, which meant a research run could slow down or interrupt real conversations — and we had no way to tell, from the outside, which was which. Now they're independent: your chat is unaffected by whatever the research job is doing, and if the research model has a bad day it simply writes nothing rather than borrowing yours.

We also tested the model properly rather than trusting its reputation. The first two we tried both failed on the thing that matters most here — one restated figures it had been told not to, and the other named a competitor's product. Neither shipped. The pair we settled on came through sixteen out of sixteen checks clean, including a test written specifically to tempt them into breaking the rules.

entries.title: Sparky now does its own research
entries.body:
Sparky can now look up what's happening in the market each day and write down what it learns, so its answers about yields and how our vault compares get better over time.

It keeps a small set of notes and rewrites them, rather than adding a new one every day. That sounds like a detail and isn't: an assistant that accumulates notes forever gets *worse* at answering, because every new note competes with the documentation that already answers you correctly. Keeping the set small is what stops that.

Every figure says which network it came from, and you'll see why that matters immediately: the alpha runs on a test network where rates are a fraction of the live market. Sparky states both and never puts them side by side as if they were choices — one is a demonstration, the other is what the same strategy earns where the money is real.

Anything Sparky writes itself is labelled as its own research and not yet reviewed by a person, the same way it already labels our documentation and these release notes. It's reference material: it never changes what you're offered, what you can sign, or your ability to withdraw.

entries.title: Sparky now learns every update on its own
entries.body:
Ask Sparky what shipped recently and it will now include the newest releases — including this one — without anyone pressing anything.

An earlier note here promised exactly that, and it turned out not to be true. Sparky could read the changelog, but only after an admin manually rebuilt its index. So each new update was published to this page and stayed invisible to Sparky until someone remembered a step nobody had been told about. We found it the obvious way: yesterday's update appeared here, and Sparky still hadn't heard of it.

Learning now happens as part of every release, and it is careful about it — an update Sparky has already read is skipped rather than re-read, so this costs nothing when nothing has changed.

We also corrected the dates on the last four entries. They were written in local time and stored as UTC, which put them hours ahead of the clock — the most recent one was showing tomorrow's date. They now read as the record they're meant to be.

entries.title: One place to manage what Sparky knows
entries.body:
Everything you write for Sparky now lives on a single page, in five clearly labelled sections: your documentation, Sparky's persona, its own research notes, the updates you publish here, and the tips that appear around the app.

They used to be spread across three separate screens with three different shapes, so keeping Sparky's answers current meant knowing which page held what. Nothing about how they work has changed — they've just been gathered in one place, and each section now says plainly what it is and who wrote it. That last part matters more than it sounds: the persona is Sparky's character rather than reference material, and it is deliberately never quoted back as a source.

Your existing links still work. The old Tips and Updates addresses take you straight to the right section, and both still have their own entries in the menu.

You'll also find a new Self-authored section. It is a preview only — nothing is being generated yet, and it says so. It shows where Sparky's own daily research will appear once we've finished designing how it works, which is a conversation about what a note is allowed to claim rather than a coding job.

entries.title: Sparky now knows what we shipped
entries.body:
Ask Sparky what changed recently and it will tell you, instead of pointing you at this page.

Until now the assistant read one set of documents and nothing else — so the updates you're reading right now were invisible to it, along with the short explainers that appear around the app. Both are now part of what it reads. The useful consequence: every future update teaches it automatically. Nobody has to remember a separate step, which means it won't be forgotten.

You'll also see clearer sourcing under its answers. Where an answer draws on something, the note now says what kind of thing it was — our documentation, a release note like this one, an explainer, or Sparky's own research. That last one matters: if Sparky is quoting itself, you should be able to see that rather than mistake it for something we wrote and checked.

entries.title: Strategies you can actually compare — and a plan that means something
entries.body:
Two screens that looked finished were quietly doing very little. Both are fixed.

**Strategies now shows you a choice.** It always promised one — "ranked against your plan", "best fit #1" — but a second option was being dropped before it ever reached the page, every single time. You'll now see the SparkPoint vault alongside supplying directly to Aave, with the actual difference spelled out: the vault manages the position and takes 10% of the yield you earn (never your principal); going direct costs you no SparkPoint fee but you look after it yourself. We'd rather tell you that than quietly hide the cheaper option.

**And it tells you what that means in money.** Not just "0.4% APY" — what that earns on your balance over a year, next to what leaving it idle earns, which is nothing. Test-network rates sit near zero and the page now says so, instead of leaving you to conclude the product doesn't work.

**Your plan can finally hold what we keep asking you for.** Sparky has been telling people to "set a mandate — how much you're willing to put at risk", and there was nowhere to put that number. Now there is. You can also say what you're saving toward and by when, and what you intend to add over time — and see how far along you are. To be clear, that last one is a note of your intention, for projections and reminders: nothing moves without you signing it.

**And you can change one thing without redoing everything.** Editing your plan used to mean re-answering every onboarding question to adjust a single setting. Each part is now editable on its own, in Settings.

A few smaller repairs came with it: the risk badge on a strategy is now that strategy's actual risk rather than a fixed number; the line about how a strategy fits your plan is now based on your plan; picking a strategy carries your choice through to the review step instead of starting over; and plans that described themselves contradictorily — "High risk (5/5), capital-preservation-first" — read correctly now, including ones saved before today.

entries.title: Sparky now notices what you do on the platform — not just what you say in chat
entries.body:
Until now, Sparky's memory only covered your conversations. Deposit into the vault from the vault page, make a swap, claim from the faucet — and as far as Sparky knew, none of it ever happened.

Now it notices. When you start a chat, Sparky quietly catches up on what you've done since you last spoke: vault deposits and withdrawals (including ones you made entirely on your own), moves you executed from its suggestions (it knows the difference — ask "did I ever act on your advice?"), swaps (sized approximately, and honestly marked as such), and faucet claims. A transaction you signed that didn't go through is remembered gently, as exactly that.

Everything it notices shows up word-for-word in Settings → Memory, right alongside the conversation notes — and Clear still means clear: erased activity stays erased, it doesn't creep back the next time you chat.

The boundary hasn't moved an inch: this is context for conversation and suggestions only. It can't approve anything, it can't make a move eligible that wasn't, and it's never involved in moving your funds — every transaction still passes the same checks and still needs your signature.

entries.title: Sparky answers straight — and admits it when something breaks
entries.body:
We spent a night putting the assistant through the same twenty questions a new user would ask, in a real browser, and fixed everything that read badly. Most of it was not the thinking — it was the answering.

**It no longer talks past you.** Ask what's in your wallet and it now tells you about your wallet: your ETH, your SRK and your idle USDC, alongside anything you have deposited. Ask what you've paid in fees and you get the actual fee schedule — plus an honest note that there is no per-wallet total to show, and why. Ask for the current APY and you get today's figure, not a lecture on what an APY is. Ask whether it can buy something for you automatically and it explains how signing really works here, instead of opening a swap.

**It knows what it is now.** Asked about SRK, the faucet, the Trust Center, the changelog, or its own memory, it used to draw a blank — once even denying it remembers anything between conversations, which it does. It can answer all of that now.

**It won't advise you into a corner.** Asked whether to put your life savings in, it declines to give financial advice, explains why concentrating everything in one place is the real risk, and offers to help you set a limit instead of handing you two things to buy.

**And when something goes wrong, it says so.** A failed turn used to look like a vague, unhelpful answer. Now it reads as what it is — a failure, with a Try again button, and a clear note that nothing was signed or changed. Refreshing the page also drops you back into the conversation you were in, the thinking steps tidy themselves away once an answer arrives, and the little internal labels that occasionally showed up above tips are gone.

entries.title: A tidier side menu — and changelog labels that stay put
entries.body:
Two pieces of housekeeping from your feedback.

The side menu is slimmer: Changelog now lives inside the Information section, and Premium and Automation have moved out of the menu entirely — into Settings, where they belong. Your plan (with its renewal date) sits under Settings → Account, and your automation session keys under Settings → Security, which now shows their real state instead of a fixed line. Nothing was removed: every page is still there, one tap deeper, and the ⌘K search still finds them by name.

And the little New / Fixed / Improved labels on these very updates will no longer occasionally vanish. Some entries were written with wording our display didn't recognise, and it responded by showing nothing — twice now. The fix is structural: labels are normalised wherever they enter the system, a check now rejects any future update written with unrecognised wording before it can ship, and the display itself will always choose a sensible label rather than none.

entries.title: The Premium pages now know you're Premium
entries.body:
Right after the first real Premium purchase was granted, its buyer noticed something silly: the Premium page still listed Free as "your current plan", and the payment page still warned they couldn't afford "the first month" — of the subscription they were already inside.

Both pages were simply never told about your plan; they showed the same thing to everyone. Now they check. If you're Premium, the plan card says so — with your renewal date — the payment page reframes itself as extending your subscription (paying again adds a month on top, it never overlaps), and the low-balance note talks about extending, not starting.

If anything ever goes wrong reading your plan, the pages fall back to the ordinary free view rather than guessing — they'll never invent a subscription you don't have.

entries.title: Premium purchases now complete — the first real one caught a day-one bug
entries.body:
The very first real Premium purchase on the alpha did everything right: the SRK payment went through on-chain, to the right place, for the right amount. Then our server fell over granting the subscription — "Unexpected error" — leaving the buyer paid-up but not upgraded. Not acceptable, and now fixed.

The cause was a one-line date-arithmetic bug in how we compute your subscription's expiry — present since the Premium feature shipped, and invisible until a real purchase exercised it. It's fixed, and we verified the fix by replaying that exact real payment: the subscription granted, backdated correctly to the original purchase.

If a purchase ever fails to grant again, your payment is never lost: every payment is verified from the blockchain itself, so a replay can always complete the grant after the fact — which is exactly what we did here.

entries.title: Sparky keeps its thinking to itself
entries.body:
While verifying the memory update on the live alpha, we caught Sparky — rarely, and only on certain phrasings — answering with its own working notes instead of an answer: the kind of behind-the-scenes reasoning you were never meant to see. Asking it nicely not to do that was already part of its instructions; clearly that wasn't enough.

So now it isn't a request, it's a rule the software enforces: any reply that reads like internal deliberation is thrown away before it reaches you, and you get Sparky's plain fallback line instead. A slightly boring answer beats a leaked one, every time.

Nothing else changed — memory, suggestions, and every safety check are exactly as they were.

entries.title: Sparky now remembers what you've done together — see and clear it in Settings
entries.body:
Until now, every new conversation started from a blank slate. Sparky could follow along within a single chat, but the moment you opened a new one it had no idea you'd ever spoken — which is a strange thing for an assistant you talk to every day.

Sparky now keeps a short running note of what you've done together: the questions you've asked, the strategies it suggested, when you looked at your portfolio. It's brief by design — a couple of lines per exchange, and only the most recent ones are kept — and it's built from what actually happened on screen rather than from a second pass of the AI guessing at a summary. Ask "what did we look at last time?" in a brand-new chat and you'll get a real answer.

You can see exactly what it remembers, and erase all of it, under Settings → Memory. The list shows the notes word for word — not a tidied-up version — because you should be able to check what the assistant is working from. Only you can see your own; there's no admin view of it anywhere.

One thing worth being plain about: this memory is context for conversation and suggestions only. It never authorises anything, it can't make a move eligible that wouldn't be otherwise, and it is never involved in moving your funds — every transaction still goes through the same checks and still has to be signed by you.

We also fixed a related quirk in the same pass: Sparky would sometimes talk about its own reference material instead of just answering ("the notes you provided don't say who I am"). It answers directly now.

entries.title: The side menu is tidier — and nothing was hidden
entries.body:
The left-hand menu had grown to ten flat entries, which made the things you actually *do* hard to pick out from the things you *read*.

Swap, Bridge, Automation and Changelog now sit at the top level, and the reference pages — Trust Center, Outcome Log, Fees, Learn and SRK — live together under a collapsible **Information** group. It starts collapsed, remembers whether you opened it, and opens itself if you land directly on a page inside it. Nothing was removed and no page moved to a new address.

The command palette (⌘K / Ctrl-K) now draws from the same list, which quietly fixed a real gap: SRK, Learn and Changelog were missing from it entirely. Searching still works with the old wording too — type "withdraw", "revoke" or "how we make money" and you'll get where you expect.

**Withdraw / Exit** stays pinned at the bottom of the menu, outside every group, exactly as before.

entries.title: Not on the list? You can now apply — instead of hitting a wall
entries.body:
Until now, connecting a wallet that wasn't on the alpha list told you so and left you there. That was the end of the road.

Now, two things happen. First, we check automatically whether your wallet holds at least **1,000,000 SRK on Ethereum mainnet** — if it does, you're let straight in on that same sign-in, no form and no waiting. If not, you get a short application: how to reach you, what to call you, and why you'd like access. A person reviews it, and you can come back any time to check the status or update your answers.

Two notes on the details. The mainnet check is a single read of your public balance — nothing is signed, nothing is spent, and if that check is unavailable for any reason you simply see the application form rather than being blocked. And whatever happens with access, the **withdraw / exit** path stays exactly where it was on that screen: getting your funds out is never behind a form.

entries.title: Premium is now 10,000 SRK per month
entries.body:
The monthly Premium price has moved from 500 SRK to **10,000 SRK**. With the new faucet that is two claims away, so it stays easy to test.

We also removed the "≈ $12.00" figure that used to sit next to the price. It was only ever illustrative — there is no exchange rate we can honestly quote for the test SRK token — and it was pinned to the old price, so it had become doubly misleading. Premium is priced in SRK, and only in SRK.

Nothing about this changes the free tier. The chat assistant, the vault, deposits, yield, swaps and withdraw-anytime are free and never require SRK.

entries.title: Get test SRK in one click — the faucet now lives on Premium
entries.body:
Trying the Premium purchase used to require SRK you had no way to get. There is now a faucet: open **Premium**, click claim, sign, and the SRK lands in your own wallet. You can claim **5,000 SRK once every 24 hours** per wallet.

A few things we were deliberate about. The amount, the cooldown and how much the faucet has left are all read live from the contract, so what you see is what the contract will actually do — not a number we typed into the page. If you have claimed recently the button tells you exactly how long is left rather than failing at signing time. And the faucet can only ever hand out SRK that was put into it up front: the SRK token has a fixed supply and no way to create more, which is why the faucet is a separate contract rather than a change to the token.

As always, you sign; SparkPoint holds nothing and cannot claim on your behalf.

entries.title: Behind the scenes: chat history is now reliably recorded
entries.body:
While verifying the previous update on the live alpha, we found that saving your conversation history could quietly fail whenever a reply contained certain punctuation — an em-dash, a curly quote — which, with an assistant that likes full sentences, was most replies. The chat itself always worked; what broke was the record of it, so a conversation you reopened later could be missing the assistant's side.

The cause was a mismatch between how we packaged the saved cards and how our database accepts text. It's fixed, we've verified real conversations now save and reopen with their cards intact, and we added an alarm so that if history recording ever fails again it announces itself instead of failing silently.

Nothing about this touched your funds or your settings — it was purely the conversation log.

entries.title: Sparky can finally introduce itself — and reopened chats keep their cards
entries.body:
Two things made the assistant feel broken, and both are fixed.

**Asking Sparky about itself got you a stock sentence.** "Who are you?", "what can you do?", "hi" — every one of them came back with the same fixed line, every time. That was not the assistant being terse; there was simply no code path that answered questions about Sparky at all, so it fell through to one hardcoded reply. It now genuinely answers, in its own voice, and an off-topic question (the weather, say) gets an honest redirect instead of a canned response.

Worth saying plainly: on this conversational path Sparky only ever **talks**. It cannot propose or build a transaction there, and it never could — that is a structural property of how the reply is built, not a rule we ask it to follow. If the model is unavailable, you get the honest short answer rather than an error.

**Reopening an old conversation used to gut it.** Your swap cards, recommendations and portfolio snapshots collapsed into placeholder text like "[proposed action: aerodrome_swap]". The cards were never actually being saved — only a one-line description of them was. They are saved now, and they come back as real, interactive cards, rendered by exactly the same code that drew them the first time.

Two details we were deliberate about. A replayed card carries the **same safety verdict it was issued with** — nothing is re-approved just because it was reloaded, and anything you act on is re-checked before you sign, as always. And conversations from before this update are untouched: they keep working exactly as they did, they simply have no cards to restore.

entries.title: Saving your plan now actually works — and it never did before
entries.body:
If you finished onboarding and pressed **Set my plan**, it failed. Every time, for everyone. We would then tell you to "check your connection and try again" — which was not only wrong, it was advice that could never have worked.

Here is what was actually happening. Every request our app makes carries a small reference tag so that if it gets sent twice by accident, we don't act on it twice. Ours was formatted incorrectly for this one request, and our server rejected it on sight — before it ever got as far as reading your plan. So no plan has ever been saved through onboarding. The server was right to refuse; the mistake was entirely on the app's side, and that is where we fixed it.

**Your plan now saves, and you can change it and save again as often as you like.** Each save is recorded as a new version, so your earlier plans aren't overwritten or lost.

We also fixed the part that annoys us more than the bug did. When a save fails now, we tell you **the actual reason** the server gave, instead of assuming it was your internet. We only mention your connection when we genuinely could not reach the server at all. Blaming you for our error is a bad habit for software to have, and we would rather not have it.

As always: your plan is guidance for what Sparky may suggest. It authorises nothing, and it can never move your money.

entries.title: We stop asking you to start over every time you come back
entries.body:
If you had already set up your plan, the sign-in screen kept offering **"Start onboarding"** as its main button every single time you returned — as though we had never met you. The screen simply never checked whether you already had a plan, and because sign-ins last a week and returning wallets are sent straight there, most people saw it constantly.

It now recognises that you have a plan and offers **"Continue to app"** instead, with a quieter link if you actually do want to look at or redo your plan. If you haven't set one up yet, nothing changes — you'll still be invited to start.

One deliberate detail: if we can't tell either way (the check is slow, or it fails), we show you the old wording rather than guessing. This screen is the door into the app, and a convenience check is never allowed to lock it.

entries.title: No more "Premium subscription" prompt on things that were never paid
entries.body:
Reviewing some of Sparky's suggestions — supplying directly to Aave, for instance — brought up a screen headed **"Confirm: Premium subscription"**. Understandably, people read that as: this move is behind a paywall.

It is not, and it never was. There is no paid tier on any suggestion Sparky makes. What had happened is far more boring: when the app has no way to carry out a particular kind of move for you, it was falling back on the wrong placeholder screen — and the one it picked happened to be the Premium one. A purely technical gap was being dressed up as a commercial one, which is exactly the sort of thing that makes a product feel like it's up to something.

You now get a plain note saying what's true: Sparky can suggest that move, but the app can't carry it out for you yet, so there's nothing to sign here. No button, because there is nothing to buy and nothing to approve. You're free to act on the idea yourself wherever you normally would.

Deposits, withdrawals and swaps are unaffected — they were always real, and still are. And as ever, nothing moves without your signature.

entries.title: The fee breakdown now shows every layer — including the ones that aren't ours
entries.body:
On the Morpho vault our fee summary used to end with the phrase "+ Morpho curator fee". That named a cost without ever telling you how big it was, which is not much better than not mentioning it.

It now shows three separate lines: **what we charge**, **what the underlying vault charges**, and **the net after both**. We split them deliberately rather than showing one combined number, because the two are not the same kind of thing. Ours we set and can answer for. The other belongs to a vault curator we don't control, who can change it without asking us. Blending them into one figure would hide that distinction — and hide which half could move.

One detail we want to be pedantic about: **"we haven't read this yet" and "there is none" are now shown differently.** If a fee is genuinely zero it says so. If we simply haven't been able to read it, it says that instead. Those look the same on a screen if you're careless, and treating an unknown as a zero is how a product ends up quietly making a promise it never checked.

The net yield line follows the same rule. On our test network Morpho publishes no yield data at all, so it reads "unavailable" rather than 0% — because 0% would be a number we made up.

entries.title: A real Morpho vault is now live on our test network — the stand-in is gone
entries.body:
Until today the "Morpho" vault you could see on our test network was a demo. Its underlying contract was a mock we had written for testing, and anyone on that network could have moved its share price. We closed it to new deposits last week and said so plainly. Withdrawals were never affected.

It has now been replaced by the real thing: a vault built on **Morpho's own audited contract**, created by Morpho's own factory, putting funds to work in a genuine Morpho lending market. We wrote none of the code that holds the money — that is the point. Our job is to configure and curate it, not to reinvent custody.

Some specifics we think you should be able to check rather than take on trust:

- **Control sits with a 2-of-3 multisig, not one key.** Ownership, curation and the emergency role were all handed to it, and every sensitive change is behind a 3-day delay you can watch on chain.
- **We permanently gave up the ability to block your shares or your money.** Morpho's contract lets an operator install "gates" that can stop shares or assets from moving. We renounced those controls irreversibly, so no future decision by us — or by anyone — can put one back. Nothing we do can ever stand between you and your exit.
- **We charge no fee on it yet.** The vault's own performance and management fees both read zero on chain right now.
- **Its yield figure is shown as unavailable, not as 0%.** Morpho's data service doesn't cover test networks at all, so we would have to invent a number to show one. We would rather show nothing than something untrue.

One honest caveat worth stating: this vault does **not** keep a "high-water mark". On the Aave vault, if your balance dips and recovers you pay nothing until you're back above your previous best. Here, a gain after a loss still counts as a gain for that period — so it can be charged even while you're below your previous high. That difference is not in our favour to explain, which is exactly why we're explaining it.

This is on our test network only. Nothing changes for real funds.

entries.title: Two small internal safety checks, tightened
entries.body: Housekeeping you won't see, told anyway. First: links we attach to our own announcements are only ever supposed to point back into the app, and we found a way one could have been written that looked internal but actually sent you to another site. Only our own team can write those links and none of them ever did — we closed the gap anyway. Second: before any of our internal notes go into the knowledge Sparky reads from, they're scanned so a secret can never be filed by mistake; that scan now also recognises a wallet key written in a slightly different format. While testing a third check we found it would have wrongly flagged ordinary sentences as if they were a recovery phrase, so we deliberately left it out rather than ship something that blocks honest writing — we'd rather the guard be right than look thorough. Nothing here changes what you see or do, and none of it ever touched your funds.

entries.title: Our fee wording now follows each vault's real rules — not one blanket promise
entries.body:
Until now every screen described our performance fee the same way: 10% of your gains, charged only above your "high-water mark" — meaning if your balance dipped and recovered, you paid nothing until you were back above your previous best. That is exactly true of the Aave Yield Vault you can use today, and nothing about it has changed.

It will not be true of every vault we add. We're preparing to offer vaults built on Morpho's own audited contracts, and those contracts don't keep a high-water mark. On one of those, a gain that comes after a loss IS charged, even if you're still below your earlier peak. What stays the same either way: we never charge anything on your deposit, never charge in a flat or falling period, there is no management fee, and nothing is ever held back to let you withdraw.

So we've stopped writing the fee one way everywhere. Each vault now states its own terms — on its page, in the fee breakdown, and in the confirmation you sign — and the wording is generated from the vault's actual contract rather than typed out by hand on each screen. We're doing this before any such vault exists rather than after, because a fee promise you'd have had to discover was wrong isn't a promise. We also corrected a related line that called our 20% fee ceiling "immutable": that's true of our own vault, where it's fixed in the contract's code, but on a Morpho-built vault the limit is held by our multi-signature wallet and a 3-day delay instead — stronger than a policy, weaker than code, and now described as what it is.

Separately, we fixed two links that pointed at the wrong network's block explorer, including one on the page whose whole job is helping you verify and exit on-chain.

entries.title: We tightened the price protection on swaps started from chat
entries.body: When you start a swap from a chat suggestion, the card carries a "max slippage" setting — the worst price you're willing to accept before the trade is cancelled. We found that the assistant could propose that number without a ceiling, so in an unusual case it could have been set far too loose, which would let you get a noticeably worse price than the quote you saw. We've capped it at 3% in three separate places: where the assistant proposes it, in the data format itself, and again in the app before the trade is built. If no value is proposed you get the normal 0.5% default, and you can still set your own on the Swap page as before. Nothing changes in how swaps look or work for you, no funds were ever at risk from our side (we hold no keys and you sign every swap yourself), and we have no sign this was ever triggered — we found it ourselves while double-checking our own security notes, and we'd rather tell you than not.

entries.title: Getting ready for real money: we hardened how we read the blockchain
entries.body: Nothing changes on your side today — this is groundwork, and we'd rather tell you about it than not. Before real money is ever involved we went back through the part of SparkPoint that reads the blockchain and prepares your transactions, looking for places where it could be pointed at the wrong network and not notice. We found some, and closed them. The service now proves which network it is talking to before it will quote you a number or prepare a move, and refuses to answer at all rather than answer from the wrong place. We also made hands-off moves work out the network fee at the moment you make them instead of using a fixed figure that only suited our test network, tightened a check so an out-of-date move can't be sent, and made sure one person's prepared transaction can never be handed to somebody else. Your funds, the vault, and the withdraw-anytime guarantee are untouched by all of this — every one of these changes can only ever make us MORE careful, never less. Still test network only; the real-money launch has its own separate review to pass first.
entries.cta_label: See what we can and can't do

entries.title: We closed deposits on the test Morpho vault — your withdrawals stay open
entries.body: The second vault in the picker on our test network — "SparkPoint Morpho USDC" — was never a real Morpho vault. It was a stand-in we built so the picker had something to show, and we've now found that the stand-in can be poked by anyone on the test network: a stranger could move its share price or tie up the cash available to withdraw. Nobody's real money was ever involved, but that's not a vault we're willing to keep taking deposits into, so we've retired it. Deposits are closed. Withdrawals are NOT — if you hold shares in it, it still shows in your portfolio and you can take your money out at any time, exactly as before. That's a rule we hold ourselves to: we may decide to stop taking money in, but we never decide when you can take money out. The reason we built a stand-in in the first place was that we believed Morpho didn't run on test networks. We checked again properly and that was wrong — Morpho is live on Base Sepolia. So the replacement won't be another stand-in; it will be the real thing. We're also changing how we build these vaults: instead of writing our own vault contract to sit on top of Morpho's, we'll configure Morpho's own audited contract for it. Less of our code between you and your money.

entries.title: We ran hands-off automation for real — and it works on-chain
entries.body: A quick, honest follow-up to the hands-off automation news below. We didn't just ship it and hope — we ran the entire flow end-to-end on our test network: a scoped session key signed and executed a real vault move on-chain with no signing prompt, exactly as designed. That live test also surfaced one rough edge in how a move was packaged for the network; we fixed it, so the very first hands-off move you make goes through cleanly rather than bouncing. Nothing changes on your side and there's nothing to do. As always, this is test-network only, every move is still an explicit button you press (we never act on our own), and you can revoke instantly. We're sharing this because we'd rather show our work than just claim it's done.

entries.title: Hands-off automation is here — approved moves, no signing prompt
entries.body: This completes the feature we've been building toward: if you grant Sparky a scoped session key, an approved, in-scope vault move can now run WITHOUT you signing each one. On an approved suggestion you'll see a new 'Let Sparky do it' button — but only when you have a live grant AND set it up on this device. Two things we want to be plain about. First, YOU stay in control: 'hands-off' means no signing prompt, not no you — every move is still a button you press; Sparky never moves on its own, and you can revoke instantly (that now works even if our servers are down). Second, your automation key is generated on your device and stored ENCRYPTED there — you unlock it once per session with a quick signature that authorizes no move; we never hold it. This is on our test network only for now. If you don't want any of this, do nothing — every move stays manual and you sign each one, exactly as before.

entries.title: The plumbing for hands-off moves now runs end-to-end
entries.body: A follow-on to the automation news below. Behind the scenes, an approved automated move now flows through our normal safety pipeline the exact same way a move you sign yourself does — it's decoded, the recipient is pinned to YOUR account, it's simulated, and it must pass every on-chain rule (allowlist, per-transaction and lifetime caps, slippage, expiry) — the only difference is which key signs it. Once your session key signs, we simply relay it to the network and give you a live status you can track, and we double-check the signed move matches exactly what was built before recording anything (so nothing can be swapped in under the hood). This is still test-network only and still fully bounded by the on-chain leash you hold. The one remaining piece is the in-app switch that signs these moves for you automatically — that's what turns this on for real, and it's next.

entries.title: The Trust Center now shows more of our contracts
entries.body: A small transparency addition. The Trust Center's contracts list now also includes the vault factory (which only deploys our branded vaults, never touches funds) and the swap router behind the user-signed swap page. We also surface our extra vaults there — clearly marked as user-signed and, for now, testnet demos that wrap a mock Morpho vault, so nothing is dressed up as more than it is. As always these are all read live on-chain and verifiable on Basescan.

entries.title: The emergency kill-switch is now a real 2-of-3 multisig
entries.body: A meaningful safety hardening. The vault's emergency pause used to be controllable by a single deployer key; it's now governed by a dedicated 2-of-3 multisig (a Gnosis Safe) — so pausing new deposits, or changing fees/caps, takes 2 of 3 independent signers plus a timelock delay, and the original single key has fully given up that power. We proved the new multisig works on-chain (a pause then immediate un-pause) before locking it in. None of this can ever touch your withdrawals — you can always exit, paused or not. You can see the guardian and this 2-of-3 controller live on the Trust Center.

entries.title: The bell now gives you a heads-up before things change
entries.body: Your notifications used to tell you about things that already happened. Now they also watch for changes worth knowing about ahead of time: when the vault is getting close to its deposit limit, when the Aave lending rate moves meaningfully, and when a genuinely new kind of opportunity becomes available to you. Each alert is triggered by a real, verifiable reading — the vault's on-chain balance against its cap, the live rate, the set of strategies that clear your guardrails — never a made-up notification, and you're only told once per genuine change — never when the assistant simply re-orders the same suggestions, and never on ordinary back-and-forth right around a threshold. Turn any category on or off in Settings → Notifications. (Session-key expiry alerts arrive alongside automation later, and email / push notifications still aren't part of this.)

entries.title: Our operator dashboards now run on real numbers too
entries.body: Following on from wiring our internal money-view to the live blockchain, we've now connected the rest of our internal operator dashboards — user growth, the onboarding funnel, risk mix, and top depositors — to real data computed from the system's own records, replacing the last of the placeholder sample figures. These are internal tools, so your own dashboards are unchanged; wallets are only ever shown in a pseudonymized form, and we never present a made-up number as real.

entries.title: Hands-off automation just went from planned to proven
entries.body: One of our biggest planned features — letting Sparky make approved rebalancing moves for you WITHOUT asking you to sign each one — was blocked on a hard technical problem for weeks. It's now solved and proven on our test network: we built a scoped, capped, time-limited 'session key' you can grant, and demonstrated a real automated move (a vault deposit) that went through end-to-end with no per-move signature — while staying fully bounded by the on-chain rules. Crucially, YOU keep the leash: the key can only ever do the specific things you allow, up to the caps you set, until it expires, and you can revoke it instantly and directly on-chain without us. The opt-in screen to turn this on for yourself is coming next — for now the Automation page still shows a preview.

entries.title: More of what we show is read straight from the blockchain
entries.body: A behind-the-scenes integrity improvement. We swept our internal monitoring views and replaced the last placeholder sample figures with numbers read live from the blockchain — the vault's real total value locked, its deposit-cap headroom, and its live pause/guardian safety state. It reflects a rule we hold ourselves to: never show a made-up number dressed up as real. Your own dashboards are unchanged — this is about the tools we use to watch the system on your behalf.

entries.title: Your notifications are real now — no more sample data
entries.body: The bell (top right) and the Notifications page now show your REAL activity instead of sample data. Each notification is derived from what actually happened on-chain — a deposit or withdrawal confirming, a realized win or loss on a position, or a transaction that reverted — never a made-up alert. The unread count is real, and your category toggles in Settings → Notifications now actually filter what you see. Alerts that watch for a change over time (the vault filling up, a rate moving) are coming in a follow-up; email / push delivery and session-key alerts come later too.

entries.title: Your signed moves link to their outcome more reliably
entries.body: A small reliability improvement to the credibility loop. After you sign a move, we tell the app to record it so it can later show how that specific move performed. If the blockchain is briefly a beat behind, we now wait for your transaction to confirm and quietly retry a couple of times — so the link between your move and its outcome sticks, without you doing anything. As always this happens in the background and never holds up signing or your ability to withdraw; your wallet is the only thing that ever signs.

entries.title: Every AI suggestion now gets a durable, trackable identity
entries.body: A small under-the-hood improvement to the credibility loop. The moment the AI shows you a suggestion, we now give it a durable identity — so if you act on it later, we can reliably tie it back to the exact advice you saw and the outcome it produced. Nothing changes in what you see; it just makes the 'did this advice actually pay off?' tracking more robust. And if our advice records are ever briefly unavailable, your recommendations still load as normal — this is an advisory index that never touches your funds.

entries.title: See which AI suggestions actually paid off — in your Outcomes
entries.body: Your Outcomes page now has a 'By recommendation' view. Each AI suggestion you acted on is listed with what it actually did — how much you put in, your realized and unrealized gains or losses, and a win / loss / open label — traced to the exact transaction you signed. Open any one to see why the AI suggested it, plus its annualized return once the position is closed. Every figure is reconstructed live from the blockchain and the vault's share price — never a stored or made-up number; a deposit blended with others is honestly labelled as your share, not a pretend split. Losses show as plainly as wins.

entries.title: Safer confirmation of the moves you sign
entries.body: We tightened how we record a transaction you've signed: we now confirm it actually exists on-chain and exactly matches the move you reviewed before we log it — instead of trusting the reference we're handed. If the transaction hasn't shown up on-chain yet, we simply ask to try again in a moment rather than record anything unverified. Your funds are never affected either way — this only makes our record of your activity provably accurate.

entries.title: See how the AI's past suggestions actually performed
entries.body: When you act on an AI suggestion, we now link it to what it actually did on-chain — so your Outcomes can show whether that specific piece of advice made or lost money, not just your position overall. Every figure (what you put in, realized and unrealized gains, an annualized return, win/loss) is reconstructed live from the blockchain and the vault's share price — never a stored or made-up number.
